title: A gas valve risk register

blocks.text: A gas utility keeps a register of its line valves. For each valve it has the age today, the Weibull curve of its type (`beta`, `eta` in years) and the cost of one failure `cof` ($k). Each valve in the register is working today. A failed valve is replaced, so the register uses the chance of *at least one* failure in the coming year, as in lesson 1.1.2. That is why this practice uses PoF although the lesson counts expected failures from its last rule on: the expected count is for an asset that is repaired and kept, and can fail again in the same year, while a valve that fails here is replaced, not repaired, so the question is whether it fails at all.

items: `risk(v)`: valve `v`'s expected failure cost in the coming year, $k;
`rank_by_risk(valves)`: the valves' ids, highest risk first.

blocks.text: Write the risk as a formula in the lesson's notation first. The tests compute each valve's chance of failing with `scipy.stats.weibull_min`. About five lines.

cases.says: valves with the same curve and age rank by the cost of a failure
an old valve that is still working is ranked by its chance of failing given that it works today
a valve likely to fail can outrank one whose failure costs more
a valve's risk is its chance of failing in the coming year times the cost of a failure

origin.section: PoF, CoF and Risk Rank Assets Differently, and a Risk Matrix Blurs Them

concepts: ranking by the product differs from ranking by either factor or by matrix cell
